I added terabytes of storage to my Asus ROG Ally thanks to my NAS and iSCSI

By  Dylan Turck

Try something different:

When the Asus ROG Ally debuted, it delivered the kind of performance handheld enthusiasts had been waiting for. With its AMD Ryzen Z1 Extreme APU, 120Hz 1080p screen, and a Windows 11 environment, it felt like a pocket-sized gaming desktop. But it also came with the same flaw as most handhelds: very limited storage. With modern AAA games often exceeding 100GB, the internal SSD fills up quickly, even on the 1TB model. While microSD cards offer extra storage, they’re slower, less durable, and can bottleneck higher-performance games.

✕ Remove Ads

I needed something faster and more robust, without cracking open the device to replace the SSD. That’s when the thought occurred of using my NAS to store all of my Ally’s games. By using the iSCSI protocol, I added terabytes of reliable, network-based storage to my ROG Ally and added my full library to the handheld.

The storage problem with gaming handhelds

Smaller devices have less storage

✕ Remove Ads

The ROG Ally, like most gaming handhelds, struggles with storage. Between operating systems, essential apps, updates, and a few major game titles like Baldur’s Gate 3, Forza Horizon 5, or Call of Duty, you’ll quickly hit the storage ceiling. MicroSD cards can be helpful, but they’re not ideal. Even the fastest UHS-I cards top out at around 100MB/s and sequential reads, and write speeds are often far lower.

✕ Remove Ads

Plus, microSD storage doesn’t handle long-term heavy usage as well as SSDs do, especially under constant read/write cycles from modern games. In my experience, load times increased and performance was inconsistent. Rather than shuffling game installs or spending hundreds on a larger internal SSD, I decided to make better use of my existing NAS. That’s where iSCSI came in.

What is iSCSI?

Why should you use it over SMB or NFS

✕ Remove Ads

iSCSI stands for Internet Small Computer Systems Interface. It’s a network protocol that allows your device to access remote storage over Ethernet or Wi-Fi as if it were a locally attached hard drive. For Windows, a remote iSCSI “target” behaves like any internal or external drive. That distinction matters. Unlike typical network shares (such as SMB or NFS), which most game launchers won't accept for installations, an iSCSI volume appears in Windows as a real drive with a letter (e.g., G:).

That means Steam, Epic Games Launcher, EA App, Battle.net, and even Xbox for PC can all install directly to it with no special configuration. Even better, iSCSI uses block-level communication, which generally offers faster and more consistent performance than file-level protocols like SMB. For gaming, where fast asset loading is key, this makes a noticeable difference.

✕ Remove Ads

You might wonder why not just use a network share instead. After all, both methods involve connecting to remote storage, right? The issue is compatibility and performance. Most PC game launchers refuse to install games to SMB or NFS shares, they expect local or external drives. Even if you manage to trick them into it, you risk corrupted installs and worse performance. By contrast, iSCSI provides a native disk experience. Once mounted, Windows treats it no differently than a physical SSD or HDD. This makes it far more stable and reliable for heavy-duty use like gaming.

How it changed my ROG Ally experience

And how it can change yours too

After connecting my Ally to an iSCSI volume hosted on my Synology NAS, I instantly added 2TB of usable, game-ready storage. My NAS is connected to my router via 2.5GbE, and my Ally connects via USB-C Ethernet or Wi-Fi 6, depending on where I’m playing. The performance was surprisingly strong. Over wired gigabit Ethernet, I saw sustained read and write speeds of around 90–110 MB/s, on par with, and sometimes better than, what I was getting from my high-end microSD card.

✕ Remove Ads

More importantly, it was consistent. Games installed to the iSCSI volume ran smoothly, with load times just slightly longer than those stored on the internal SSD. I played everything from Hogwarts Legacy to Control with minimal performance penalties. While it’s not the ideal solution for competitive games, it’s more than adequate for open-world RPGs, indie games, and most other titles.

✕ Remove Ads

If you already have a NAS, or you’re comfortable setting one up, iSCSI is one of the best ways to expand the ROG Ally’s storage without compromising portability or speed, and more importantly, without breaking the bank. It turns your handheld into a network-attached game console, perfect for home use and LAN setups. The ROG Ally is a strong competitor in the gaming handheld market and with iSCSI and a good NAS, it finally has the storage to match.

This setup isn’t a mobile solution. Once you leave your home network, your iSCSI drive goes with it (unless you configure a secure VPN tunnel, which adds latency and complexity). But for home gamers or enthusiasts, it’s a fantastic upgrade.

Is it worth all the work?

The pros and cons

✕ Remove Ads

iSCSI allowed me to scale beyond the limits of the Ally’s internal SSD and microSD support, without cracking open the case or spending money on pricey upgrades. With a wired connection or strong Wi-Fi signal, the iSCSI volume performs as well as or better than high-speed SD cards. Game launchers see the volume as a native drive, which means no workarounds or hacks are needed. The same volume can be used by other PCs on my network.

✕ Remove Ads

There are, however, a few cons as well. The iSCSI volume is only available when connected to your local network (or a VPN). You can’t access it on the go. While not rocket science, iSCSI isn’t plug-and-play. You’ll need to configure both your NAS and Windows to make it work. NAS drives may spin down when idle, and waking them can introduce a few seconds of delay. You can tweak this with power settings, but it’s worth noting.

✕ Remove Ads

A great setup, if you already have a NAS

The ROG Ally is a phenomenal handheld PC that’s slightly hampered, like most handhelds, by limited internal storage. iSCSI solves that in a clever, effective way, leveraging your network to expand storage without sacrificing performance or compatibility. It's not the simplest solution, but it's powerful, flexible, and entirely within reach if you already own a NAS. For gamers who like to tinker, this upgrade is worth every second of setup.
